claim: With a material lead of a piece or more, most of the opponent's remaining chances come from tricks with the queen. Taking the queens off the board removes many of them at once.
notes: DRAFT - author to review. Original wording as general chess advice; not taken from any book.
advice: When you are a piece or more ahead, look for a way to trade queens, even if it costs a pawn.

claim: Most games at club level are decided by a move that allowed a simple capture, check or mate. Looking at every forcing reply before moving catches most of them.
notes: DRAFT - author to review. Original wording as general chess advice; not taken from any book.
advice: Before you let go of the piece, look at every check and capture your opponent would have after your move.

claim: Opening trouble usually comes from spending moves on things other than development and king safety, such as early pawn grabs or moving one piece several times.
notes: DRAFT - author to review. Original wording as general chess advice; not taken from any book.
advice: In the opening, bring a new piece into play with most moves and get your king safe before you start an attack.

claim: A player who reaches the late middlegame of a three-minute game with under a minute left can only play simply, so it pays to set a time budget early.
notes: DRAFT - author to review. Original wording as general chess advice; not taken from any book.
advice: In 3+0, try to leave the opening with at least two minutes; if you are below one minute later, choose safe, simple moves.

claim: A slow slide often means the opponent has a plan and you have not noticed it. Naming their next goal in a few words makes the defence concrete.
notes: DRAFT - author to review. Original wording as general chess advice; not taken from any book.
advice: When your position keeps getting a little worse, stop and name what your opponent wants to do next, then decide how to stop it.
